artworks.title: Castor on the Niobid Krater
artworks.description: On this celebrated Attic red-figure calyx-krater, now in the Louvre (G341), Castor is shown as a youthful horse-tamer, identified by the inscription of his name beside the figure. As one of the Dioscuri, the mortal twin brother of Pollux and brother of Helen and Clytemnestra, Castor was renowned in antiquity as a master horseman and athlete; the painter accordingly equips him with horse and spears. The vase, attributed to the workshop of the Niobid Painter at the height of the early Classical style, is one of the few ancient images to label the hero by name.

artworks.title: The Rape of the Daughters of Leucippus
artworks.description: Rubens depicts the violent abduction of Phoebe and Hilaeira, the daughters of Leucippus, by the Dioscuri — Castor and Pollux. The mounted twins seize the two struggling women in a swirling, diagonal composition charged with Baroque energy, the rearing horses and entangled limbs forming a single muscular knot of bodies. The myth was a favorite subject for demonstrating the heroic, kinetic ideal of the male body, and Rubens' canvas, now in the Alte Pinakothek in Munich, became the defining image of the episode in European art.

artworks.title: Statues of Castor and Pollux
artworks.description: This pair of Roman marble statues presents the Dioscuri as standing nude youths, each accompanied by his horse and wearing the distinctive pilos, the egg-shaped cap recalling the eggshell from which the twins were said to have hatched. Castor and Pollux were widely venerated as protectors — of sailors, horsemen, and guests — and were honored across the Roman world with paired cult images such as these. The matched, mirrored poses emphasize the inseparable bond of the twins, the central theme of their myth.

artworks.title: Sarcophagus with the Abduction of the Leucippides
artworks.description: This Roman marble sarcophagus relief, now in the Vatican Museums (Inv. 2796), carves the carrying-off of the daughters of Leucippus by Castor and Pollux across its front. The twins, on horseback, sweep up the two women amid a crowded frieze of figures, a scene of struggle and rescue well suited to funerary art, where the Dioscuri's role as saviors and their own movement between mortality and the stars carried hopes for the deceased. Castor, the mortal twin who shared immortality with his brother, embodied the consoling promise of survival beyond death.
